title: CFA Alternatives 5: Farmland and timberland - two assets that both yield and appreciate
subtitle: A compound source of return, the ability to defer the harvest, and why they correlate so little with equities
whyItMatters: This is the part of the natural resources Learning Module that almost nobody studies, because it never shows up in the financial press. But it contains a mechanism no other asset class has - and that mechanism is why the large funds allocate here.
openingQuestion: Where does the return from a timberland investment come from?
openingOptions: Only from selling the timber at harvest
From three sources: timber volume, timber price, and land value
Only from the land appreciating over time
From annual rent paid by whoever works the concession
explanation: These three sources are independent of one another, and that is what makes timberland unusual. The first - biological growth - is something no other asset class has: the trees keep growing whatever financial markets are doing, so the quantity of the asset rises without anybody doing anything. That source also creates a genuine option: when timber prices are low the owner defers the harvest and the trees keep growing; when prices are high they cut sooner. Very few assets let the owner choose when to sell while the intrinsic value rises during the wait - and that property is what explains the low correlation with equities.

summary.keyIdea: Timberland has three independent sources of return - biological growth, timber price, land value - and the trees keep growing while you wait for a better price, which makes the timing of the sale a genuine choice.
summary.commonMistake: Ignoring physical risk. Fire, pests and extreme weather cannot be diversified away inside a financial portfolio.

application.title: Why it suits a long-horizon fund
application.message: A long growth cycle means never being forced to sell into a short-term price cycle - an advantage only a patient investor can actually use.

sections.text: Farmland and timberland are two assets that both generate cash and appreciate, but the return mechanism of timber contains one component no other asset class has.
The three independent sources of return from timberland

items: Biological growth: the trees keep growing whatever financial markets are doing - the quantity of the asset rises without anybody doing anything.
Timber price: the price per unit moves with demand from the construction and paper industries.
Land value: the worth of the ground beneath the forest in its own right.

sections.label: A real option
sections.text: When timber prices are low, the owner defers the harvest and the trees keep growing; when prices are high, they cut sooner. Very few assets let you choose the moment of sale while intrinsic value rises during the wait.

Leasing the land to a farming operator gives an even cash flow, close to an inflation-linked bond. Operating it yourself yields more but takes on the whole of the harvest risk, the crop price and the input costs. These two choices differ in the nature of the risk, not merely in the level of return.

sections.label: A word of caution
sections.text: The low correlation with equities that reports like to quote comes partly from a genuine property of the asset, and partly from the smoothing effect of appraisal-based valuation. Do not bank the whole of that number as a diversification benefit.
Three sources of return, and only one of them depends on financial markets

sections.title: Why timberland has such an unusual return structure
sections.subtitle: Three near-independent sources, compounding over the holding period

concepts.def: The trees keep growing whatever financial markets are doing. The quantity of the asset rises with no work and no transaction required. This is the only source that is genuinely uncorrelated with equities.
Driven by the construction cycle and industrial demand. This is the volatile part, and it is also the part the option to defer the harvest can manage.
The underlying worth of the ground, independent of what stands on it. In many markets this is the largest source of appreciation over long cycles.

sections.label: A real option, not a figure of speech
sections.text: When timber prices are low, the owner defers the harvest and the trees keep growing - meaning the cost of waiting is negative, because the asset adds volume while you wait. When prices are high, they cut sooner. Very few assets let the holder choose the moment of sale without a penalty: equities do not multiply while you hold them, and rental property still costs money to maintain. This is the genuine difference this asset class offers.

sections.label: And this is where it gets oversold
sections.text: The low correlation with equities that reports like to quote comes from two sources, and only one of them is real. The real part is the biological property above. The unreal part is that value is set by periodic appraisal rather than by daily trading - an asset revalued only once a quarter, by a process that looks back at past prices, will always produce a return series smoother than reality and a correlation lower than reality. This is appraisal smoothing, and it shows up in every unlisted asset class, not only in forestry.

lines: The trees grow while you wait.
That is what makes this asset class different - and it is also the part most easily oversold.

realWorldExample.description: There are two ways to hold farmland and they produce very different risk profiles. The lease model: the landowner collects a fixed rent and the tenant carries all of the harvest and crop-price risk - a steady cash flow, close to a bond. The operating model: the owner farms it directly or shares the output, so they capture the whole upside of a good year at a good price and absorb the whole loss of a failed harvest. The same field, two structures, two fundamentally different assets.

quiz.question: Which source of return exists in timberland and in no other asset class?
options: Annual rent paid on a steady schedule by the operating party
Land value rising with the local property market
Timber prices rising with demand from construction and paper
Biomass growing regardless of what financial markets do
quiz.explanation: The other two are price movements, something plenty of other assets also offer. Biomass is physical growth in the asset itself: the trees add volume whether markets are open or shut, and nobody has to trade anything for it to happen. Rent from an operator is a contractual income stream rather than growth in the asset, and it is just as available on farmland or on commercial property.

quiz.question: What advantage does the right to defer the harvest give?
options: Waiting for a better price while the asset keeps growing
A tax exemption in any year when no harvest takes place
The right to sell the harvesting rights on to a third party
A guarantee that timber prices revert to a long-run mean
quiz.explanation: This is rare: for most commodities, waiting costs you storage. With timber, waiting makes the asset larger. Deferring a harvest carries no tax relief of its own, the ability to on-sell rights depends on the contract rather than on biology, and nothing about a standing forest guarantees prices come back - the option is valuable precisely because they might not.

quiz.question: Why does timberland show low correlation with equities?
options: Because the state fixes timber prices to a schedule set each year
Because biomass grows on a biological clock, not a financial one
Because timberland is not traded on any market whatsoever
Because forest value is only reappraised once every ten years
quiz.explanation: Be careful with the reasoning that says 'it does not trade, therefore it is uncorrelated' - that is the appraisal smoothing effect, not genuinely low correlation. Timber does trade, timberland changes hands regularly, and valuations are refreshed far more often than once a decade. The real answer is biological: the volume of wood grows on its own schedule.

quiz.question: A farmland lease has a risk profile closest to which of these?
options: Commodities, because value tracks crop prices directly
Equities, because the income swings with crop prices from year to year
Bonds, because the cash flow is fixed and the tenant bears crop risk
Bank deposits, because there is no risk to the principal at all
quiz.explanation: Shifting harvest risk onto the tenant is what turns a real asset into a near-fixed income stream. Under a lease the landowner's return does not move with the season, which is exactly what separates it from a commodity or an equity claim. It is not a deposit either: the land can fall in value, and the tenant can fail to pay.

quiz.question: On the same plot, what changes when you move from leasing it out to operating it yourself?
options: The liquidity of the asset improves considerably
The market value of the plot rises by a correspondingly large amount
The tax due on income from the land is waived entirely
The owner now bears crop and commodity price risk directly
quiz.explanation: This is the easy thing to miss when comparing two farmland investments: the same asset class does not mean the same risk profile. Switching from a lease to own-operation does not make the land more liquid, does not change what a buyer would pay for the plot, and waives no tax - it moves the harvest and the price of the crop out of the tenant's account and into yours.

keyTakeaways: Timberland has three independent sources of return: biological growth, timber price, land value
Biological growth is physical growth in the asset - no other asset class has it
The right to defer the harvest: wait for a better price while the asset keeps growing
Leased farmland behaves like a bond; operating it yourself takes on the harvest risk
Careful: the 'low correlation' of a thinly traded asset may be nothing but appraisal smoothing

practicePrompt.question: A timberland fund reports a positive return in every one of ten years, including the year equities fell 30%. How should you read that?
options: Timberland is a risk-free asset over a long enough horizon
Check whether the reported values are smoothed by appraisal
The fund has certainly been manipulating its reported figures
This proves forestry deserves a large weight in the portfolio
practicePrompt.explanation: Two genuine effects are stacked on top of one another here and they have to be separated. Biological growth really does not care what the stock market does, so part of that positive return is real. But timber prices and land values do move, and they are recorded through infrequent appraisals - so the stability in the report is exaggerated by exactly the mechanism covered in the previous lesson.
